item.title: OpenAI Solves Navier-Stokes Problem Amid Controversy With Mathematicians
item.description:
OpenAI Solves Navier-Stokes Problem Amid Controversy With Mathematicians

OpenAI has announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems established by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. The development has been accompanied by disputes involving NYU professor Tristan Buckmaster regarding the company’s conduct and the use of researcher data.

⚙️ Key details

OpenAI utilized an advanced, unreleased model to find the solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids. The process involved:

  • Compute resources: Tens of millions of dollars of compute.
  • Agent scale: Roughly 10,000 agents.
  • Timeframe: 88 hours.

🔍 Overview

Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge, a researcher at Anthropic, had been pursuing a proof for the Navier-Stokes problem. OpenAI stated it decided to test its model after hearing researchers were making progress on Millennium Prize problems.

Controversies have emerged regarding the interaction between OpenAI and the researchers:

  • Collaboration offers: Buckmaster alleges he was offered “unlimited compute” and the opportunity to be the sole author of OpenAI’s announcement paper if he excluded Alpöge from the work. Bubeck acknowledged offering resources to help Buckmaster complete his proof or take over the writing of OpenAI’s paper, stating that OpenAI has made similar arrangements with other mathematicians.
  • Competing interests: Bubeck stated that Alpöge’s affiliation with Anthropic was a sticking point, questioning how OpenAI could have an internal project involving an Anthropic employee.
  • Data usage: Buckmaster questioned if OpenAI benefited from his use of Codex. While OpenAI spokesperson Laurance Fauconnet categorically denied that prompts from the last two months influenced the system, the company previously acknowledged it could not rule out that data derived from product use was used to improve the model.

💡 Why it matters

The Millennium Prize problems are considered among the most formidable challenges in mathematics, with each carrying a $1 million bounty.

#OpenAI #Mathematics #NavierStokes #AIagents #MillenniumPrize

Source: OpenAI just wants to win

item.title: Researchers Establish New Bayesian Regret Bounds for Thompson Sampling in Bandit Convex Optimization
item.description:
Researchers Establish New Bayesian Regret Bounds for Thompson Sampling in Bandit Convex Optimization

Researchers Bakhtiari, Lattimore, and Szepesvári (COLT 2025) have established new Bayesian regret bounds for Thompson sampling (TS) applied to bandit convex optimization problems.

🔍 Overview

The study differentiates between monotone and non-monotone ridge losses in convex optimization. The researchers provide theoretical bounds on the performance of Thompson sampling under these two distinct conditions.

⚙️ Key details

The findings establish the following regret bounds:

Loss Type Bayesian Regret Bound
Monotone ridge losses $\tilde O(d^{5/2}\sqrt n)$
Non-monotone convex ridge losses $\tilde O(d^{9/2}\sqrt n)$

🧩 How it works

  • Monotone Case: The proof utilizes a single-removal John-ellipsoid dichotomy.
  • Non-Monotone Case: The researchers demonstrate that the John-ellipsoid dichotomy fails for non-monotone links via an explicit twelve-point configuration. Instead, they employ an $O(d^2)$ cardinality bound for “uninformative” configurations.
  • Mathematical Argument: The bound relies on a Boolean rounding argument, which posits that a 0-1 matrix within $1/(4r)$ in max-norm of a rank-$r$ matrix has a rank of at most $2r-1$.
  • Verification: The team constructed $d(d+1)$ uninformative losses, demonstrating that the cardinality bound is tight up to constants in the large-diameter-to-gap regime.

💡 Why it matters

While these bounds have been established, it remains an open question whether the $d^{5/2}$ dependence observed in the monotone case can be retained for non-monotone scenarios.

#ThompsonSampling #BanditOptimization #COLT2025 #MachineLearningTheory

Source: Thompson Sampling for Non-Monotone Convex Ridge Bandits: Monotonicity Is Not Needed for Polynomial Regret

item.title: OpenAI faces new criticism over possible use of unpublished math research
item.description:
OpenAI faces new criticism over possible use of unpublished math research

OpenAI’s recent announcement of a result on non‑sofic groups has drawn fresh criticism from mathematicians who say the company may have used unpublished research in its training data.

🔍 Overview

  • OpenAI announced a result involving non‑sofic groups, a class of infinite mathematical structures that cannot be approximated by finite ones.
  • The result was one of ten highlighted in the company’s announcement last month.

🧩 Concerns from the research community

  • Mathematician Andreas Thom posted on Mastodon that his earlier interactions with ChatGPT might have contributed to the success.
  • Thom and colleague Gábor Kun had prior work on non‑sofic groups that OpenAI acknowledged as heavily used.
  • Thom wrote to OpenAI researchers Sébastien Bubeck and Mark Sellke (a statistician at Harvard) asking whether his conversations were part of the training data; the reply only addressed direct access, not inclusion in the broader training corpus.
  • Thom said researchers cannot reverse‑engineer OpenAI’s training pipeline, and he urged the company to disclose datasets and usage terms.

⚙️ OpenAI’s response

  • The company amended its write‑up after criticism for not initially crediting Thom and Kun.
  • In a separate statement about its Millennium Prize Navier‑Stokes solution, OpenAI said it did not see any specific user data, but added that “while unlikely, we cannot rule out that de‑identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.”
  • OpenAI has not commented to The Verge on the latest concerns.

💡 Why it matters

  • Thom called it “ethically indefensible” for a model to improve on non‑public research and then race the same researchers to publication without consent or credit.
  • Researchers fear such practices could push mathematics toward secrecy if rumors of breakthroughs trigger competitive races with well‑resourced AI firms.
Person Role / Affiliation
Andreas Thom Mathematician (raised concerns)
Gábor Kun Mathematician (co‑author of prior work)
Sébastien Bubeck OpenAI researcher (contacted)
Mark Sellke Statistician at Harvard (contacted)
Tristan Buckmaster Mathematics professor, New York University
Levent Alpöge Anthropic researcher (collaborated with Buckmaster)

#OpenAI #Mathematics #AIEthics #TrainingData

Source: Mathematicians want proof OpenAI didn’t use their work

item.title: OpenAI claims Navier–Stokes solution amid credit dispute with NYU and Anthropic
item.description:
OpenAI claims Navier–Stokes solution amid credit dispute with NYU and Anthropic

Today OpenAI announced that its agents have produced a proof that the full Navier–Stokes equations can break down, a result that would solve one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.

🔍 Overview

  • OpenAI announced agents solved Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem.
  • The problem is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000.
  • Solutions carry a $1 million prize; before today only one other Millennium Problem had been solved.
  • Navier–Stokes equations describe fluid flow and it was unknown whether they could break down to an impossible state such as infinite velocity.

⚙️ Technical Details

  • The proof shows the full Navier–Stokes equations can break down.
  • It was produced with an internal OpenAI model that outperforms the Astra model released the previous week.

Model comparison

Model Note
Astra Released last week; considered impressive
Internal OpenAI model Dramatically outperforms Astra; used for Navier–Stokes proof

⚖️ Controversy

  • Accusations that OpenAI used AI‑assisted work of NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge without credit.
  • Buckmaster posted a proof of a simplified Navier–Stokes breakdown on Mastodon; he and Alpöge had worked for almost a year using publicly available models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
  • OpenAI denied that its agents accessed Buckmaster and Alpöge’s transcripts or that employees trained on those transcripts; Mark Chen reiterated the denial.
  • Buckmaster’s document describes two options presented by OpenAI employees: (1) let Buckmaster/Alpöge post their work and OpenAI post its solution the next day, or (2) collaborate on a paper that would exclude Alpöge because of his Anthropic affiliation.
  • OpenAI also stated it does not plan to claim the million‑dollar prize.

💡 Why it matters

  • Solving Navier–Stokes would settle a major open question in fluid dynamics and mathematics.
  • The approach builds on work pioneered by mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez‑Zoroa, which experts consider promising.
  • The dispute raises questions about attribution and transparency when AI models are trained on external contributions.

#OpenAI #NavierStokes #MillenniumPrize #AIethics

Source: What OpenAI’s latest controversy tells us about the future of math
